data.title: Solar Eclipses Through Time and Science

excerpts.text: Long ago, people watched the bright sun vanish from the sky in the middle of the day. They believed a giant celestial dragon was swallowing the glowing orb whole. To scare the beast away, villagers gathered in the streets and banged loudly on bronze drums and pots. After a few minutes, the sun would always return to its place in the heavens. The elders nodded sagely and declared the deafening noise had successfully chased the monster off.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun. This alignment blocks the light of the Sun from reaching our planet entirely or in part. Observers in the path of totality can see the solar corona, which is the outermost atmosphere of the star. Scientists calculate the exact path and timing of these astronomical events years in advance. Special protective solar viewing glasses must be worn to prevent eye damage during the observation.
